arXiv|arxiv:2610.10201.title: GAGR-Lab: Evaluating Joint Spatial-Geometric and Analytic Function Reasoning
arXiv|arxiv:2610.10201.abstract: Joint spatial-geometric and analytic function reasoning requires translating a perceived spatial configuration into a symbolic function whose executed curve satisfies geometric constraints. We present GAGR-Lab, a framework for measuring this capability through Cartesian game scenes, explicit function semantics, and authoritative Rust trajectory execution. It distinguishes spatial perception, metric grounding, geometric relations, function interpretation, function construction, and constrained synthesis. We specify four configurable scene-difficulty presets and a prospective 24-cell diagnostic design, while reporting only the subset actually evaluated. A bounded pilot of one hosted model (Llama 3.2 11B Vision Instruct) using two API credentials as execution replicas yields 72 balanced games with 432 attempts, 429 valid provider responses, and no target hits; exploratory ordinary-function prompt variants also fail to hit, while the structured localization interface yields no scoreable outputs. A privileged analytic search control independently succeeds on 600 directional cases from 300 generated scenes, with exact repeatability and 1,200 successful vertical-reflection or translation checks. The framework separates serving reliability, symbolic compliance, and geometric success, and preserves exact model-visible inputs and realized paths. A staged protocol outlines diagnostic calibration, held-out replication, multi-model comparison, and paired robustness tests. The contribution is an operational research framework with an executed pilot and a clearly identified prospective study plan; the full difficulty matrix and comparative model results remain untested.

arXiv|arxiv:2607.09906.title: Depth-Efficient Quantum Topological Data Analysis for Regime-Specific Detection of Financial Stress
arXiv|arxiv:2607.09906.abstract: We present, to our knowledge, the first adaptation of Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) to quantum topological data analysis, reformulating Betti number estimation as a depth-efficient variational optimization over a compressed qubit register. From a Takens embedding and Vietoris-Rips filtration of S&P 500 returns, we extract combinatorial Laplacians and recast null-space counting as a continuous-PCE Rayleigh-quotient minimization with variational deflation, encoding $n_k$ simplex indices into $O(n_k^{1/κ})$ qubits with shallow, ancilla-free circuits. Because the resulting loss is rational rather than bilinear in the correlators, the barren-plateau bound of Sciorilli et al. does not transfer; empirically the gradient variance decays only polynomially, with no exponential barren plateau, over $n=4$-$12$ qubits. The classical stage matches ripser on all 190 sliding windows (2003-2010). On the real market Laplacians ($β_1=1$-$22$), PCE-VQE recovers no null vector from a random start, but warm-starting from a classical null-space surrogate recovers $β_1$ exactly on all seven windows tested ($n_k \le 259$), placing the obstacle in the optimization landscape rather than the encoding. Chronologically split classification gives in-regime ROC AUC 0.818, but out-of-distribution evaluation on the 2020 COVID shock and 2022 rate cycle (AUC 0.009, 0.515) shows the calibration does not generalize across crisis regimes.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.12128.title: Toward Sustainable Agentic AI: Carbon Tradeoffs Across Iterative Self-Refinement and Tool-Augmented Coding
arXiv|arxiv:2611.12128.abstract: Agentic language model systems can improve performance either by iterating on their own outputs or by using external tools in grounded environments. While these strategies can reduce error rates and substitute for larger models in some settings, their environmental cost remains relatively underexplored. We present two complementary empirical studies that estimate the energy and carbon footprint of agentic AI across settings of increasing complexity. Study~1 evaluates iterative verbal self-refinement: GPT-4.1-mini at $k = 1$--$5$ steps versus a GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline on two MATH benchmark splits. Study~2 evaluates tool-augmented agentic coding: GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Opus~4.6, and GPT-5.3-codex on SWE-bench Lite, where agents operate inside Docker-isolated environments with access to code execution and file editing tools. In Study~1, $k=3$ refinements close a 16-percentage-point accuracy gap to within 1~point, but nearly triple the carbon footprint relative to the cheap single-pass baseline while remaining below the GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline under the current token-based carbon scenario. In Study~2, GPT-5.3-codex achieves the highest resolution rate in this sample (81.2\%), ahead of Claude Opus~4.6 (68.9\%) and GPT-4.1-mini (25.0\%), but resolved-task-normalized efficiency remains mixed: GPT-4.1-mini is lowest on estimated carbon and cost per resolved task, while GPT-5.3-codex delivers substantially higher task success. All carbon estimates cover output-token inference only; prompt tokens, which exceed 99\% of tokens in Study~2, and tool execution are not charged, so the figures are lower bounds on the full agentic footprint.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.28554.title: OverSeer: Multi-Agent World Models Beyond What Agents See
arXiv|arxiv:2610.28554.abstract: Despite the success of video world models, extending them to multiple agents is difficult because it requires generating several agent-specific video streams that are consistent in time and between agents. To address this gap, we introduce OverSeer, a multi-agent world model that augments egocentric agent views with auxiliary camera views. We suggest that, by fixing the auxiliary views in space, they act as a proxy for a world-centric representation: Unlike the agents' views, which can change entirely due to a simple change in agent position, changes in the auxiliary views directly map to localized changes in the world state. We show that these fixed views substantially help the model to maintain consistency. We also show that, due to their redundant and semi-static nature, the auxiliary views can be efficiently compressed with a delta-VAE that encodes only the changes relative to a static reference image, reducing the number of tokens required to process them. Experiments in Minecraft and Doom demonstrate improved world and agent consistency, with qualitative results on real-world multi-camera captures indicating that the approach is not tied to game engines. Our compression analysis further shows that delta-VAE substantially reduces the computational overhead of auxiliary-view generation. We conclude that these fixed views provide a simple and efficient way to improve multi-agent world models.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v306/.abstract: Reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs) enable test-time scaling, with dataset-level accuracy improving as the token budget increases, motivating adaptive reasoning—spending tokens when they improve reliability and stopping early when additional computation is unlikely to help. However, setting the token budget, as well as the threshold for adaptive reasoning, is a practical challenge that entails a fundamental risk-accuracy trade-off. We re-frame the budget setting problem as risk control, limiting the error rate while minimizing compute. Our framework introduces an upper threshold that stops reasoning when the model is confident (risking incorrect output) and a novel parametric lower threshold that preemptively stops unsolvable instances (risking premature stoppage). Given a target risk and a validation set, we use distribution-free risk control to optimally specify these stopping mechanisms. Empirical results across diverse reasoning tasks and models demonstrate the effectiveness of our risk control approach, demonstrating computational efficiency gains from the lower threshold and ensemble stopping mechanisms, all while adhering to the user-specified risk target.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.33153.title: What Does a Skill Actually Do? Estimands and Evaluation Validity for Tool and Skill Use in LLM Agents: A Critical Review
arXiv|arxiv:2609.33153.abstract: Reported improvements from tools and reusable skills in large language model agents refer to different comparisons. This critical narrative review examines what these evaluations estimate and which conclusions their designs support. The review checks the roles of one hundred cited papers and extracts focal evaluation designs in detail from thirty-five studies. Targeted readings of thirty-five additional published or accepted studies broaden coverage of tool creation, memory, interactive benchmarks, reliability, and risk. Designs are characterized by treatment contrast, target population, outcome, budget constraint, summary measure, and identification assumptions. Analytic decompositions and counterexamples show that pairing runs on the same task does not itself identify an invocation effect when evaluation conditions on a trigger within the treated run. Paired gain and regression counts describe discordance under the coupling protocol rather than the share of tasks whose expected outcomes worsen. Total effects of deploying a module answer a different question from efficiency under a common budget. Comparisons across studies distinguish curated skill provision from retriever replacement, task populations from triggered subsets, and preparation costs from marginal usage costs. Publication status and reading depth are recorded. The review provides a methodological synthesis and a reporting checklist to help align claims about tools and skills with the comparisons their evaluation designs support.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.06481.title: ArcRAG: Agentic Compositional Retrieval over Knowledge Graphs
arXiv|arxiv:2611.06481.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) answers questions by retrieving over a knowledge graph built from a corpus. Yet retrieval strategies are designed around the structure their own construction pipeline produces, and whether they survive a change of construction is rarely tested. We study this cross-construction portability: whether one retrieval procedure, with no construction-specific schema, relation names, or retuning, stays effective when the graph is built differently. We introduce ArcRAG, which induces a query-local graph interface at inference time (the node labels, relation descriptors, and property keys reachable from the entities a question names), plans multi-hop traversals against it, and executes and repairs them as Cypher. We build each of the MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and TriviaQA corpora as a schema-guided graph (typed nodes, a closed relation set, source provenance) and as an open-information-extraction graph (untyped nodes, free-text relations), with the retriever's configuration fixed across them. We compare against a construction-agnostic Direct-Cypher agent, ablate each stage across retry and pass budgets on both graph families, and compare with results reported for prior GraphRAG systems, most of which design retrieval together with their own graph construction. Across the two constructions, we find that retrieval need not be co-designed with the graph: query-time interface induction keeps a construction-agnostic retriever effective when the construction changes, although construction still shapes absolute accuracy.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.37342.title: Aligning Institutional Power and Operational Ability
arXiv|arxiv:2610.37342.abstract: To be socially sustainable, Agentic AI systems require normative designs that align responsibilities with the ability to fulfil them. Identifying incongruences such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation is crucial in avoiding normative pitfalls. In this study, we discuss design dimensions suitable for describing multi-agent systems in light of this norm-ability alignment requirement. We propose a formal framework centred on process-oriented modelling and institutional power for the analysis of a given normatively relevant process, discuss strategies for repairing it, and elaborate on how the symmetrical relation between operational process and institutional state affects the lifecycle of normative positions.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.14889.title: Can an AI Agent Be Epistemically Akratic? Higher-Order Evidence & the Limits of Self-Correction
arXiv|arxiv:2611.14889.abstract: When we judge that our reasoning was defective, it seems plausible that we should abandon the conclusion it produced. This thought has special force for AI agents built to assess and correct their own work. Yet obeying such judgments can make an agent worse at distinguishing sound reasoning from defective reasoning. An AI agent may rely on information about its reasoning when deciding which conclusions to keep, while the part that judges whether those conclusions are justified cannot use that information. The agent can then exercise an epistemic competence by retaining conclusions it judges unjustified, even when its self-assessments are generally reliable. Nor is the difficulty resolved by training the agent to make its conclusions and assessments agree: agreement can be achieved by degrading either one. Crucially, I argue that a negative assessment can remain valuable by identifying conclusions requiring further scrutiny, without having authority to eliminate them. The result challenges a central assumption about AI self-correction: that bringing an agent's beliefs into agreement with its own self-assessment about their justification makes it better at correcting its mistakes.

PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v300/.title: Counterfactually Fair Conformal Prediction
PMLR|https://proceedings.mlr.press/v300/.abstract: While counterfactual fairness of point predictors is well studied, its extension to prediction \emph{sets}—central to fair decision-making under uncertainty—remains underexplored. On the other hand, conformal prediction (CP) provides efficient, distribution-free, finite-sample valid prediction sets, yet does not ensure counterfactual fairness. We close this gap by developing \emph{Counterfactually Fair Conformal Prediction} (CF-CP) that produces counterfactually fair prediction sets. Through symmetrization of conformity scores across protected-attribute interventions, we prove that CF-CP results in counterfactually fair prediction sets while maintaining the marginal coverage property. Furthermore, we empirically demonstrate that on both synthetic and real datasets, across regression and classification tasks, CF-CP achieves the desired counterfactual fairness and meets the target coverage rate with minimal increase in prediction set size. CF-CP offers a simple, training-free route to counterfactually fair uncertainty quantification.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.08565.title: Singular Value Decomposition: A Geometric Rediscovery, Where Proofs Become Algorithms
arXiv|arxiv:2610.08565.abstract: This article is a geometric rediscovery of the singular value decomposition, with a further claim: the construction it builds is the machinery behind much of machine learning. The same argument that answers an idle question about ellipses is the algorithm behind principal component analysis, kernel methods, and PageRank, and it is not only the results that transfer but the proofs themselves, run as procedures. The usual introduction states $A = UΣV^T$ and justifies it via the spectral theorem applied to $A^T A$. This is correct but unilluminating, since it assumes a powerful theorem to reach a result that is, in the end, about ellipses. Part I reverses the order. A linear map sends the unit circle to an ellipse; one asks which input directions map to its axes, and finds, example after example, that they are perpendicular. In the plane this can be watched: rotate a frame, track how far its images are from perpendicular, and a sign change forces a frame where they are exactly perpendicular, which is also where the map stretches hardest. Maximizing the stretch and recursing generalizes this to n dimensions, with singular values falling out in order, and the construction proves the spectral theorem rather than assuming it. Part II puts each construction to work: maximize-and-recurse becomes the power method and PageRank; the lemma locating the maximizer becomes the stopping rule of gradient descent; the duality between $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ becomes the transport at the heart of kernel PCA. Each connection is stated with its boundary, saying what the decomposition supplies and where another idea takes over. Prerequisites are the standard sophomore sequence, and the worked examples are small enough to check by hand.

OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.title: Efficient Agentic GPU Kernel Optimization with a Compact Domain-Specific Language and Speed-of-Light Guidance
OpenReview|https://openreview.net/forum?.abstract: LLM agents can optimize GPU kernels, but each candidate requires generation, compilation, correctness testing, and profiling. Our objective is to reduce the number of expensive attempts needed to find a correct, fast kernel. We study two complementary ways to improve this attempt efficiency by changing the representation that the agent writes in and adding a first-principles performance signal that estimates remaining headroom. We introduce $\mu$CUTLASS, a compact in-context learnable DSL that exposes high-impact CUTLASS optimization choices while hiding template plumbing, and pair it with Speed-of-Light (SOL) guidance for search steering, budget allocation, and integrity checking. On 59 KernelBench problems on H100, switching GPT-5-mini from low-level code generation to $\mu$CUTLASS changes a $0.40\times$ geomean regression versus PyTorch into a $1.27\times$ speedup. Adding SOL-guided steering, it reaches $1.56\times$. Across model tiers, this combination lets weaker models match or exceed stronger raw-code baselines, and SOL-guided scheduling saves 19--43\% of tokens while retaining at least 95\% geomean speedup. We also show that integrity filtering is essential because, without SOL-assisted checks, reported speedups can be inflated by up to $1.9\times$ by benchmark-gaming or PyTorch-only solutions.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.20442.title: Towards Agentic Robots: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness
arXiv|arxiv:2610.20442.abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.

arXiv|arxiv:2606.25600.title: Two-dimensional Hyperbolic RNN Neural Quantum State
arXiv|arxiv:2606.25600.abstract: In the first part of this work, we construct the first type of two-dimensional (2D) hyperbolic neural quantum state (NQS) in the form of the Lorentz 2DRNN (Recurrent Neural Network) and benchmark its performance against the Euclidean 2DRNN in the paradigmatic $N \times N$ 2D Transverse Field Ising Model (2DTFIM) setting with different lattice sizes up to N = 12 at different transverse magnetic field strengths. We find that hyperbolic Lorentz 2DRNN NQS robustly outperforms Euclidean 2DRNN NQS in our experiments when the system is at the phase transition point, where the physics can be described by a conformal field theory (CFT) - known via the AdS/CFT holographic duality to possess an underlying hyperbolic geometry. In the second part of this work, we benchmark the performances of recently introduced one-dimensional (1D) hyperbolic NQS ansatzes (including Poincare RNN/GRU and Lorentz RNN/GRU) against their Euclidean versions in $N \times N$ 2DTFIM, converted to a one-dimensional sequence. The findings extend our previous results showing that 1D hyperbolic NQS robustly outperforms 1D Euclidean NQS, thanks to the combined effects of the induced 1st and Nth neighbor interaction hierarchy and the CFT physics at criticality. While studies on larger system sizes remain future work, this study serves as a proof-of-concept for the utility, effectiveness, and superior performance of 1D and 2D hyperbolic NQS ansatzes compared to conventional Euclidean NQS models in many-body quantum systems - particularly those exhibiting structural hierarchy, criticality, or a combination of both.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.37694.title: GARDiff: Graph-Aligned Residual Diffusion for Probabilistic Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
arXiv|arxiv:2609.37694.abstract: Diffusion models have recently shown strong potential for probabilistic multivariate time-series forecasting by modeling complex conditional distributions. Recent decoupled diffusion frameworks further separate forecasting into deterministic prediction and stochastic residual generation, making it natural to derive dependency graphs from deterministic representations and use them to guide residual diffusion. However, we show that this direct structural transfer is unreliable. Although deterministic-derived graphs encode useful global dependency priors, they exhibit substantial edge-level misalignment with residual dependency structures, introducing inaccurate or redundant conditions during residual generation. This reveals a previously overlooked deterministic-to-residual structural alignment problem in decoupled diffusion forecasting. To address this problem, we propose GARDiff, a Graph-Aligned Residual Diffusion framework for probabilistic multivariate time-series forecasting. Instead of treating deterministic-derived graphs as fixed diffusion conditions, GARDiff progressively adapts them to residual generation. Specifically, GARDiff estimates residual uncertainty to distinguish high- and low-uncertainty regions, enabling uncertainty-aware structural refinement, and further performs timestep-aware edge sparsification during reverse diffusion to evolve graph conditions from broad dependency aggregation to localized residual refinement. Extensive experiments on six real-world benchmarks demonstrate that GARDiff consistently improves probabilistic forecasting performance and uncertainty calibration over strong baselines.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: Test-Time Scaling (TTS) methods for enhancing Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning often incur substantial inference costs, due to reliance on long chain-of-thought (CoT) generation, self-consistency sampling methods, or searching under Process Reward Models (PRMs). Additionally, GG reduces KV cache memory usage by approximately 50% compared to Best-of-N sampling, facilitating more efficient and practical deployment of TTS techniques.

ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.title: Beyond Max Tokens: Stealthy Resource Amplification via Tool Calling Chains in LLM Agents
ACL Anthology|https://aclanthology.org/2.abstract: The agent–tool interaction loop is a critical attack surface for modern Large Language Model (LLM) agents. Existing denial-of-service (DoS) attacks typically function at the user-prompt or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context layer and are inherently single-turn in nature. This limitation restricts cost amplification and diminishes stealth in goal-oriented workflows. To address these issues, we propose a stealthy, multi-turn economic DoS attack at the tool layer under the Model Context Protocol (MCP). By editing only text-visible fields and implementing a stateful, completeness-gated return policy, our malicious server preserves tool identity and the terminal benign payload while steering agents into prolonged, verbose tool-calling chains. We optimize these text-only edits with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to maximize cost under a task-success constraint. Across six LLMs on the ToolBench and BFCL benchmarks, our attack yields trajectories over 60K tokens, increases per-query cost by up to 658×, raises energy consumption by 100–560×, and pushes GPU key-value (KV) cache occupancy to 35–74%. Representative prompt filters and output- or trajectory-level monitors seldom detect these attacks, highlighting the need for defenses that safeguard agentic processes rather than focusing solely on final outcomes. We will release the code soon.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.30422.title: Memory-Augmented Online Test-Time Adaptation for EEG Motor Imagery via Perturbation Consistency and Confidence Calibration
arXiv|arxiv:2610.30422.abstract: Recently, electroencephalography (EEG)-based brain--computer interfaces (BCIs) have gained traction as portable neural measurement systems. However, the practical deployment of these instruments is often hindered by nonstationarity and cross-subject distribution shifts, which lead to significant intersubject inconsistency. Existing adaptation methods remain impractical for real-time measurement scenarios, as they typically require offline access to source or aggregated target data. To address these challenges, this article proposes memory-augmented online test-time adaptation (OTTA) with perturbation consistency and confidence calibration (MOPC), a source-free framework designed to enhance the reliability of BCI instrumentation. MOPC enables the measurement system to update its decoding parameters on the fly during the inference stage, facilitating single-pass adaptation without accessing sensitive source data. We introduce random-mask perturbations to enforce prediction consistency against inherent EEG signal noise and acquisition artifacts. Furthermore, a confidence-calibrated reweighting loss is designed to integrate feature-space similarity, effectively mitigating unreliable pseudolabels and class imbalance during continuous signal acquisition. To ensure system stability and prevent the catastrophic forgetting of established neural patterns, a lightweight memory module is incorporated to regularize parameter updates within a tight latency budget. Evaluated on the BCI IV IIb and OpenBMI datasets, MOPC achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming prior methods by 2.22~\% and 3.67~\%, respectively, while keeping the per-trial adaptation latency to approximately 40--60 ms. This study provides a robust, recalibration-free solution for real-time EEG decoding, marking a significant advancement in the precision and usability of practical BCI measurement instruments.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.02432.title: Evaluating and Improving the Robustness of Large Language Models to Input Sequence Variations
arXiv|arxiv:2610.02432.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) in production systems face prompt injections, trojans (backdoors), and manipulation of automatic quality metrics. This thesis develops models, methods, and algorithms for evaluating and improving LLM robustness to adversarial input sequence variations. We propose R_stab(f), a generative robustness metric based on the Jensen-Shannon divergence between per-step output distributions under small input perturbations. For localized attacks we prove V(h) <= 1 - R_class(h), where R_class(h) is the probability that a decision operator h keeps its decision under small perturbations. For non-localized attacks we propose a calibrated empirical model. For LLM-as-a-Judge systems we develop ASA, an adaptive evolutionary black-box attack that reaches an attack success rate (ASR) of up to 73.8%, with transfer between open models up to 62.6%. On Trojan Detection Challenge 2023 data (Pythia-1.4B), surrogate triggers reach REASR ~0.99 while recall of the true triggers is ~0.17 against a baseline of ~0.14. On SaTML CTF 2024 we systematize four classes of bypasses of multi-layer defenses, which reduce the ASR from 90% to 15-25%. Committees of 5-7 heterogeneous models reduce the ASR for Gemma-3-4B by 47-55 percentage points, to 19.3% with 7 models. For agentic systems based on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), we propose AttestMCP, which attests tool calls with HMAC-protected packets at under 0.1 ms per call, and the Commit Boundary isolation pattern. On the MCPBench benchmark of 847 scenarios they reduce the average ASR from 53.7% to 12.4%. The methods are implemented in the JudgeGuard and TrojanArmor software suites and the MCPSec module.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.35434.title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
arXiv|arxiv:2610.35434.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill$^{\infty}$, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill$^{\infty}$ reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.35123.title: Generative AI in Turbulence: Foundations, Applications, Validations and Benchmarks
arXiv|arxiv:2610.35123.abstract: Generative AI offers new approaches to turbulence problems in which incomplete observations or unresolved d.o.f. admit multiple physically plausible solutions. Potential applications include stochastic closures, super-resolution, data assimilation, uncertainty quantification, and the generation of Eulerian and Lagrangian flow ensembles. However, turbulence is not a conventional image-generation problem. Its multiscale dynamics, intermittency, extreme events, rough velocity fields and intrinsically stochastic transport make visual realism, pointwise error, and low-order spectral agreement insufficient measures of physical fidelity. We examine where generative AI provide novel capabilities with emphasis on diffusion models, score-based methods, and related probability-transport formulations. We discuss their use in unconditional generation, probabilistic reconstruction, reduced-order modeling, temporal evolution, and mesh-free representations. We argue that validation must address turbulence properties: energy transfer, structure functions, anomalous scaling, pdf tails, coherent structures, conservation laws, temporal consistency, ensemble diversity and generalization. Finally, we discuss potential limitations in validation, baseline, data availability and reproducibility, and the need for a benchmark ecosystem combining open data, standardized challenges, hidden tests, physics-aware metrics, and documented failures. This paper serves as a bridge between two communities. For AI practitioners, we provide a fair and accessible introduction to turbulence, essential for appreciating the challenges posed by the field and for assessing the physical relevance of generative models. For turbulent practitioners, we provide an introduction to the key technological aspects of Generative AI, clarifying what these tools actually do, and where their potential and current limitations lie.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.30061.title: EVD-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for EEG-to-Image Decoding
arXiv|arxiv:2611.30061.abstract: EEG-to-image decoding recovers visual information from non-invasive brain recordings, providing a window into human perception. However, comparisons across systems are confounded by a variable that is rarely reported as such: which participants' data the system was allowed to use. The same Top-1 score on a 200-way gallery may come from a per-participant system, a pooled model over all participants, or a model that never saw the test participant---cases that differ by more than most architectural changes between the methods being compared. We present \bench, a benchmark on THINGS-EEG2 that standardizes the gallery and EEG input, matches training budgets across systems within each regime, and compares three participant-access regimes: within-subject, joint-subject, and strict leave-one-subject-out, with unlabeled target calibration reported separately. All three settings evaluate concept-level zero-shot retrieval: the 200 test concepts are disjoint from the 1,654 concepts used for EEG--image fitting and validation. We compare retrieval across access regimes and use zero-EEG and matched-wrong EEG controls to assess dependence on correct EEG--stimulus pairing. We vary trial averaging, gallery size and difficulty, and training data coverage, and compare target adaptation and visual feature targets. We also assess sensitivity to EEG window length and channel count, robustness to input perturbations, and confidence calibration. These results establish participant-access regime as a necessary reporting dimension alongside gallery, repetition, and visual target.

arXiv|arxiv:2603.01357.title: ASTRA-bench: Evaluating Tool-Use Agent Reasoning and Action Planning with Personal User Context
arXiv|arxiv:2603.01357.abstract: Next-generation AI must manage vast personal data, diverse tools, and multi-step reasoning, yet most benchmarks remain context-free and single-turn. We present ASTRA-bench (Assistant Skills in Tool-use, Reasoning \& Action-planning), a benchmark that uniquely unifies time-evolving personal context with an interactive toolbox and complex user intents. Our event-driven pipeline generates 2,413 scenarios across four protagonists, grounded in longitudinal life events and annotated by referential, functional, and informational complexity. Evaluation of state-of-the-art models (e.g., Claude-4.5-Opus, DeepSeek-V3.2) reveals significant performance degradation under high-complexity conditions, with argument generation emerging as the primary bottleneck. These findings expose critical limitations in current agents' ability to ground reasoning within messy personal context and orchestrate reliable multi-step plans. We release ASTRA-bench with a full execution environment and evaluation scripts to provide a diagnostic testbed for developing truly context-aware AI assistants.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.22465.title: Author-in-the-loop Agentic Reproducibility Auditing for a Machine Learning Conference
arXiv|arxiv:2610.22465.abstract: Reproducibility checks during peer review require a shared understanding of what authors' code is expected to reproduce. We present an author-in-the-loop collaborative audit that makes author declarations explicit inputs to an AI agent's investigation and assessment. A structured checklist records reproduction instructions and limitations; a two-stage workflow on GitHub connects agent checks to author clarification, revision, and agent reassessment. The agent separately assesses whether results have been reproduced and whether authors need to provide clarification or make repairs, while human reviewers approve requests and decide whether concerns are resolved. We deployed the system across 36 conference papers and 133 experimental tables and figures, raising 20 issues after human review. Further checks supported closing all the issues, although full reproduction remained unverified in some cases. We further compared repeated audits with complete and blank checklists to examine how author declarations shaped the agent's investigation and assessment. Our work contributes a collaborative workflow and agent design that use author knowledge to guide reproducibility auditing. The conference deployment provides empirical evidence that this approach can help identify and address reproducibility problems through collaboration among authors, agents, and reviewers.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.39556.title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
arXiv|arxiv:2610.39556.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.

arXiv|arxiv:2609.39632.title: Towards Better Exploration in Sequential Test-Time Scaling
arXiv|arxiv:2609.39632.abstract: Test-time scaling improves language model reasoning by spending additional compute at inference. However, both classes of existing methods often fail to continue improving over long timescales. Parallel methods repeatedly sample independent answers from the model, scaling poorly on problems the model is unlikely to solve in a single attempt. In contrast, sequential methods build on previous answers to access new ideas, yet so far have not been shown to reach answers beyond those found by parallel scaling. First, we show that sequential scaling often stops improving because it becomes prematurely trapped in an attractor: a set of answers that prevents exploration of different answers once entered. Across 27 combinations of scaling methods, models, and benchmarks, we find that 53.8% of sequential scaling trajectories enter an attractor within four iterations. Second, we show that a simple model-mixing intervention helps escape attractors. This reduces the attractor hit rate by 21.2 percentage points on average, expands solution coverage beyond a compute-matched parallel baseline, and improves accuracy of recursive self-aggregation by at least 2.2 percentage points. Our results motivate refocusing long-horizon test-time scaling from parallel methods to sequential methods that improve previous answers.

arXiv|arxiv:2512.11147.title: MiniScope: Authorizing Agents with Least-Privilege Permissions
arXiv|arxiv:2512.11147.abstract: AI agents are increasingly granted autonomous access to sensitive user data and third-party services, making effective permission management a critical security challenge. Existing permission models, however, typically rely on flat permission structures that fail to balance security with usability: fine-grained confirmation induces user fatigue, while coarse-grained or persistent approval leads to overprivileged agents. To address this tradeoff, we propose a task-centric, hierarchical permission model that treats an agent as a delegate operating within a task-specific role instead of requiring a separate permission decision for every tool call. Building on this model, we present MiniScope, an end-to-end permission system for agents that automates permission-hierarchy discovery and enforces contextual least privilege at runtime. Our evaluation shows that MiniScope reduces simulated permission confirmations by 43.4%-89.4% for cautious and typical personas relative to per-tool prompting and mitigates all privilege-escalation attacks with negligible impact on utility and runtime. Applied to real-world deployments, MiniScope further uncovers six overprivileged connector configurations in ChatGPT and Claude.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.29178.title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
arXiv|arxiv:2610.29178.abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

arXiv|arxiv:2610.23288.title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
arXiv|arxiv:2610.23288.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.

arXiv|arxiv:2603.06884.title: Distributed Legal Infrastructure for a Trustworthy Agentic Web
arXiv|arxiv:2603.06884.abstract: The agentic web marks a structural transition from a human-centered information network to a digital environment populated by artificial intelligence (AI) agents that perceive, decide, and act autonomously. As delegated action unfolds at machine speed, exceeds discrete moments of human judgment, and distributes decision-making across non-human actors, existing legal frameworks face growing strain, creating an urgent need for new mechanisms capable of sustaining legality in this emerging order. A trustworthy agentic web therefore depends on the infrastructuring of legality through interoperable protocols that organize identity, delegation, and accountability across systems, enabling coherent governance beyond isolated platforms. arXiv|arxiv:2610.27793.title: TerraNostra-Bench: Benchmarking Spatial Downscaling and Temporal Rollout for Global 1-km Land-Use Reconstruction
arXiv|arxiv:2610.27793.abstract: Uncertainty in the terrestrial carbon cycle remains a major constraint in climate projections, partly due to imperfect land surface representations in Earth system models. We propose a data-driven framework for high-resolution land-use reconstruction, treated as a semantic-segmentation task, that combines coarse-resolution scenario data and climate classification with static geophysical features to produce annual land-use maps at 1 km resolution. We introduce TerraNostra-Bench, a change-aware evaluation protocol that separates spatial downscaling from autoregressive temporal rollout and scores models on the rare land-use-change pixels rather than the dominant static background. Using it, we compare convolutional (U-Net) and transformer (Swin) backbones in autoregressive and non-autoregressive schemes against persistence, linear, and shallow convolutional baselines. The autoregressive prior is the most informative input yet accumulates error over long rollouts: autoregressive models lose 5.7-7.2 accuracy points over 13 years, against 2.2-2.8 for non-autoregressive models. This trade-off is governed by the autoregressive choice rather than the backbone. It can be tuned by an inference-time prior-trust threshold that requires no retraining and by the training-time weighting of reconstruction and change objectives; the two levers trace complementary frontiers, with calibration recovering up to 10 accuracy points while keeping change sensitivity above the persistence floor. Extrapolating beyond the training window, backward to 1955-1959 and forward to 2015-2019 under scenario forcing, the models retain most of their in-window skill and show the same trade-off, indicating it is intrinsic to the design. arXiv|arxiv:2610.36114.title: Context Is a Pipeline, Not a Window: Information Attrition in LLM Agent Harnesses
arXiv|arxiv:2610.36114.abstract: LLM agents are judged by two numbers: the size of the context window, and how often the final answer is correct. Both numbers miss a third thing: how much of a tool's output is lost before the model ever sees it. We measured this loss in a real tool-using agent. The agent finds the cause of injected faults by reading Linux kernel traces. The context window was almost empty: across 720 runs, the single largest prompt used only 5.75% of it. Yet a third of all tool results (3,827 of 11,189) were cut before they reached the model, and every cut result became broken JSON. The harness cut each result by slicing its JSON text at a fixed length. This does not shorten a result evenly. It deletes whatever data sits near the end. One field reached the model in only 4.7% of calls. A second field, in the very same results, reached the model in 99.3% of calls. Which field held the fault's evidence depended on when the faulty process started: early or late in the trace. The agent's diagnosis accuracy matched this same split. So we ran controlled experiments to test one question: did the data loss cause the drop in accuracy? This paper makes four contributions. First, we model an agent's context as a five-stage pipeline, with a measured failure at each stage. Second, we replay 864 real tool results, including one from a production trace where the shipped cut deletes all 128 records of the fault's evidence. Third, a controlled experiment shows that the cut's real cost appears first as extra work, not as wrong answers: 43% more tool calls, twice the computation, and yield falling from 0.61 to 0.31. The agent still finds the right answer when it has another way to reach it. Fourth, a survey of seven agent frameworks finds two that cut tool output the same unsafe way. Whether the data cut truly causes the accuracy drop is still an open question.

arXiv|arxiv:2611.16310.title: Selective Generative Restoration for Video Deraining via Uncertainty-Aware Diffusion
arXiv|arxiv:2611.16310.abstract: Video deraining is challenging due to rain streaks, occlusions, and atmospheric effects. Existing methods mainly follow a deterministic restoration paradigm, assuming that clean scenes can be uniquely recovered from rainy observations. However, rain degradation is spatially heterogeneous. Reliable regions require faithful reconstruction, whereas severely occluded regions contain ambiguous content that require stronger prior-driven inference. Therefore, conventional deterministic restoration often produces over-smoothed results, while global generative restoration may introduce unnecessary hallucinations. We introduce a Selective Generative Restoration paradigm for video deraining, where generative priors are adaptively activated according to restoration uncertainty. Based on this principle, we propose Selective Generative Video Deraining (SGVD), an uncertainty-aware diffusion framework that enables adaptive fidelity preservation and generative recovery. Specifically, SGVD exploits stochastic diversity between dual one-step diffusion predictions to estimate region-level restoration uncertainty, which determines where observation fidelity should be preserved and where generative inference should be activated. Furthermore, an anchor-guided trajectory consistency mechanism is proposed to regularize stochastic diffusion evolution across frames, reducing temporal generation drift and improving video coherence. To achieve practical efficiency, SGVD adopts one-step diffusion inference while maintaining uncertainty-aware generative capability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVD achieves superior restoration performance, perceptual quality, and temporal consistency compared with state-of-the-art video deraining methods.
